name: Uruguay
summary: A small country between Brazil and Argentina, independent in 1828; an early welfare state and today one of Latin America’s most stable democracies.

terrain.value: Gently rolling grassland with low hills (cuchillas), rivers and an Atlantic and Río de la Plata coast.

climate.value: Temperate and humid, with warm summers, mild winters and rain spread through the year.

resources.value: Fertile grassland for cattle and sheep, farmland for soy and rice, forests for wood pulp and river hydropower.

disasters.value: Floods along the rivers, and droughts such as the one in 2023 that threatened Montevideo’s drinking water.

population.value: About 3.4 million people in 2024, one of the smallest in South America.

urbanisation.value: Over 90% of people live in towns and cities; almost half live in and around Montevideo, the capital.

disease.value: Good public health, with life expectancy close to 78 years and a national health system created in 2007.

migration.value: Large immigration from Spain and Italy (1850s–1930s); many emigrated during the dictatorship and the 2002 crisis.

economicBase.value: Beef, soy, wood pulp, dairy and rice exports, with tourism, banking and software services.

tradeRoutes.value: The port of Montevideo on the Río de la Plata, and trade with Mercosur neighbours, China and Europe.

wealth.value: A high-income economy since about 2013, with one of the largest middle classes in Latin America.

moneyAndTax.value: The Uruguayan peso, introduced in 1993; taxes fund wide public services and pensions.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic, elected every five years, with a General Assembly of two houses.

keyRulers.value: José Gervasio Artigas. José Batlle y Ordóñez. José Mujica.

succession.value: Free elections every five years; presidents may not serve two terms in a row.

institutions.value: Old political parties (Colorado and National) since the 1830s, the Frente Amplio from 1971 and an independent judiciary.

stability.value: A military dictatorship ruled from 1973 to 1985; democracy has been stable since its restoration.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: A small professional army, navy and air force; Uruguay sends many soldiers to UN peacekeeping missions.

majorWars.value: Uruguayan Civil War (1839–51); War of the Triple Alliance.

territoryChange.value: Borders were set by treaties after 1828; an 1851 treaty with Brazil gave Brazil some disputed northern lands.

alliancesRivals.value: A founding member of Mercosur (1991), based in Montevideo; close ties with Argentina and Brazil.

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: Free education; One Laptop per Child (2007).

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: A road network centred on Montevideo, the port, Carrasco airport and a rebuilt freight railway.

religion.value: Largely secular: church and state were separated in 1918; Catholics are the largest religious group.

languageWriting.value: Spanish (the Río de la Plata variety); a Spanish–Portuguese mix is spoken near the border with Brazil.

artsArchitecture.value: Candombe drumming of Afro-Uruguayan origin, tango (La Cumparsita, 1916) and carnival murga theatre.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class; most people are of European descent, with Afro-Uruguayan and mixed minorities.

sharedIdentity.value: Pride in democracy, secularism, the welfare state, football and shared customs such as mate.

dailyLife.value: Most people live in towns, drink mate from a gourd and share asado (barbecued beef) with family.

neighbours.value: Brazil to the north and east, and Argentina across the Uruguay River and Río de la Plata.

ideasReligions.value: Secular and liberal ideas: an early welfare state under Batlle, and legal cannabis and same-sex marriage in 2013.

colonisation.value: Part of the Spanish Empire (Montevideo founded 1724–26) until Artigas’s revolt in 1811, then ruled by Brazil until 1828.

riseSignals.value: Independence recognised by the 1828 treaty between Brazil and Argentina; first constitution in 1830.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the early 1900s under Batlle and the years since 2005 were times of strong growth.

declineSignals.value: None that define the country as a whole.

outcome.value: Still in existence as the Oriental Republic of Uruguay, one of Latin America’s most stable democracies.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
